ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Able to act, come and go, or respond without constraint: free and at ease, at liberty, or freely.
EvidenceBody: The word is attested 4,537 times in 388 allowlisted texts. Foyan Qingyuan closes an address by telling everyone to drink tea in the hall, free and at ease (堂中喫茶，自由自在). Yunmen Wenyan says that only upon arriving here can one roll up and extend freely, with response and function unimpaired (卷舒自在，應用無虧). The Yongzheng Emperor uses the result phrase “obtain great freedom” (獲大自在), while Zhean Jingfan says “unconstrained and unbound in every place; without fault at every time” (一切處自在無繫，一切時無所過患). Dahui Zonggao says that one then enters birth and death and obtains great freedom (出生入死得大自在). Other records pair freedom in birth and death with freedom in coming and going, and explicitly test whether freedom at death matches ordinary freedom amid encountered objects. Zen bends an everyday freedom word into public tests about response, movement, birth, and death, while Baizhang Huaihai warns against casually declaring a buddha free or not free. Adjective, adverb, result noun, and the repeated form “free and at ease” remain grammatical deployments of the same condition.
